title: Big-O Complexity
tagline: A single letter that tells you whether your code runs in a millisecond or longer than the age of the universe.

sections.content:
Every algorithm consumes two resources: **time** and **memory**. **Big-O notation** is the standard language for describing how those needs scale as input grows. It does not tell you exact milliseconds — that depends on hardware, language, and runtime. What it tells you is the *shape* of the growth curve: does doubling the input double the work (linear), keep it nearly the same (logarithmic), or square it (quadratic)? That shape is what matters at production scale.

Big-O is the single most tested topic in technical interviews. A candidate who looks at a nested loop and says 'that is O(n²); here is an O(n) alternative using a hash map' demonstrates exactly the algorithmic thinking teams hire for. It also helps you choose data structures — a decision that routinely makes a thousand-fold difference in production.

sections.title: Finding a Name in a Phone Book
sections.content:
Suppose you are looking for 'Yamamoto' in a paper phone book of one million names. If you read every name from page 1, that is **O(n)** — a million comparisons in the worst case. If you open to the middle and halve the search space each step (binary search), you need at most ~20 comparisons for a million entries — **O(log n)**. If for every name you find, you then search the whole book again to find their friend, that is **O(n²)**.

You do not care whether the book has thin paper or thick — those are constants. You care about how many 'open and check' operations you perform *relative to n*. Big-O formalises this by asking 'what is the dominant term as n grows toward infinity?' and dropping everything else, including constant multipliers.

Big-O describes an **upper bound** on growth rate. Formally, f(n) is O(g(n)) if beyond some input size n₀, f(n) never exceeds c·g(n) for some constant c. In practice: drop constant coefficients and lower-order terms. `5n² + 100n + 7` simplifies to **O(n²)** because n² dominates as n grows.

The common classes in order of growth: **O(1)** constant — same time regardless of size (array index, hash map get). **O(log n)** logarithmic — halves the problem each step (binary search, balanced BST). **O(n)** linear — visits every element once (linear scan, `Array.map`). **O(n log n)** linearithmic — best possible for comparison-based sorting (merge sort, `Array.sort`). **O(n²)** quadratic — nested loops over the same data (bubble sort, naive duplicate detection). **O(2^n)** exponential — combinatorial explosion (naive recursive Fibonacci, all subsets). **O(n!)** factorial — all permutations (brute-force travelling salesman).

**Best, average, and worst case** are distinct. Binary search is O(1) best case (lucky first guess) but O(log n) worst case. QuickSort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case on already-sorted input with a bad pivot. When interviewers say 'O(n log n) for merge sort' they almost always mean worst-case (or average-case where they are the same).

**Amortised analysis** averages cost over a sequence of operations. JavaScript's `Array.push` is O(1) most of the time, but occasionally the internal buffer is full and the runtime copies all elements to a doubled buffer — an O(n) spike. Because doublings are exponentially rare, the average cost per push over n operations works out to O(1). This is called **O(1) amortised** — the total cost of n pushes is O(n), so each push costs O(1) on average.

**Space complexity** follows identical notation but counts memory, not operations. Creating an output array of length n is O(n) space. An in-place algorithm using a few loop variables is O(1). Memoised recursion trading O(n) space for dramatic time savings is the canonical time-space trade-off.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: `hasDuplicateNaive` runs about n²/2 comparisons worst-case — O(n²). `hasDuplicateFast` replaces the inner loop with a Set lookup (O(1) average), reducing the whole function to O(n) time at the cost of O(n) extra space for the Set. This time-space trade-off via a hash set is the most common optimisation pattern in coding interviews. Binary search uses `>>> 1` (unsigned right shift) as a safe midpoint — avoids integer overflow in lower-level languages and is worth recognising.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Interview habit:** state your complexity *before* writing code, not after. Say 'I think this will be O(n) time and O(n) space — let me verify as I write.' Then explicitly call out nested loops (likely O(n²)) and hash-map lookups (O(1) average). When asked 'can you do better?', the answer is almost always: replace an inner linear scan with a hash set, or sort the input first to enable binary search. Knowing that O(n log n) is the lower bound for comparison-based sorting is a reliable signal of depth.

items: Big-O describes how time or space grows relative to input size n; constant coefficients and low-order terms are always dropped.
Common classes in order: **O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!)** — each is qualitatively different.
Nested loops over the same n elements are almost always O(n²); replacing one loop with a hash-set lookup reduces to O(n) at the cost of O(n) space.
O(n log n) is the theoretical lower bound for comparison-based sorting; JavaScript's `Array.sort()` meets this bound in all modern engines.
**Amortised analysis** averages cost over a sequence — `Array.push` is O(1) amortised even though occasional buffer-doubling copies are O(n).

quiz.question: What does Big-O notation primarily describe?
options: The exact number of milliseconds an algorithm takes
How an algorithm's resource usage grows relative to input size
The number of lines of code in an algorithm
quiz.explanation: Big-O describes the growth rate of time or space as input size n increases. It ignores hardware-specific constants and focuses on the shape of the scaling curve.

quiz.question: What is the Big-O time complexity of accessing an element by index in a JavaScript array?
quiz.explanation: Array index access is a direct memory offset calculation — one operation regardless of array size. That is constant time, O(1).

quiz.question: Binary search on a sorted array of n elements has which time complexity?
quiz.explanation: Binary search halves the search space with each comparison. Starting from n elements, it takes at most log₂(n) comparisons to find the target — O(log n).

quiz.question: You replace an O(n²) duplicate-detection algorithm with a Set-based O(n) version. What resource does the faster version trade away?
options: Space — the Set stores up to n elements
Time — Set operations are slower than comparisons
Nothing — it is strictly better in all ways
quiz.explanation: The Set-based approach uses O(n) extra memory to store seen elements. This is a classic time-space trade-off: O(n) space buys a factor-of-n improvement in time.

quiz.question: What is the simplified Big-O for the expression 4n² + 50n + 1000?
quiz.explanation: Big-O drops constant coefficients and lower-order terms. The dominant term is n², so the complexity is O(n²).

quiz.question: Which statement about comparison-based sorting algorithms is true?
options: O(n) comparison-based sorting is achievable for any input
O(n log n) is the theoretical lower bound for comparison-based sorting
Bubble sort is also O(n log n)
O(log n) sorting is possible if the array is partially sorted
quiz.explanation: Information theory proves any comparison-based sort must make at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Bubble sort is O(n²); O(n) sorting requires non-comparison techniques (counting sort) with input constraints.

quiz.question: JavaScript's Array.push is O(1) amortised. Why is it not simply O(1) in every single call?
options: push() always copies the entire array
Occasionally the internal buffer must be doubled, requiring an O(n) copy
push() sorts the array after inserting
push() has O(log n) internal bookkeeping
quiz.explanation: Dynamic arrays double their internal buffer when full, copying all n current elements — O(n). Doublings are exponentially rare, so amortised over n pushes the average cost per push is O(1).

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of: `for (let i=0; i<n; i++) for (let j=0; j<n; j++) { /* O(1) work */ }`?
quiz.explanation: The outer loop runs n times and for each iteration the inner loop runs n times: n × n = n² total O(1) operations. The complexity is O(n²).

quiz.question: QuickSort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case. When does the worst case typically occur?
options: When the array is randomly shuffled
When the pivot is always the median element
When the array is already sorted and the pivot is always the first or last element
When the array has an odd number of elements
quiz.explanation: A naive first/last-element pivot on a sorted array partitions into sizes (0, n-1) every time, producing n recursive levels each doing O(n) work — O(n²) total. Randomised pivot selection avoids this.

quiz.question: An algorithm allocates an output array of length n and uses an O(n log n) loop to fill it. What is its space complexity?
quiz.explanation: Space complexity counts memory allocated, not operations performed. The output array of length n is O(n) space. The O(n log n) loop describes time; the loop variables themselves are O(1) extra space.
